data.title: How Do 3 ETFs Change Your JPMorgan Chase Risk?
data.description:
A direct stake in JPMorgan Chase gives you full exposure to its own business swings. That includes firm specific issues such as what Simply Wall St flags as a risk that heavy spending on marketing, technology and artificial intelligence could grow faster than revenue and squeeze profits. Owning JPMorgan Chase inside a fund that also holds other companies limits how much any single problem or success moves your overall portfolio, and also trims the upside from one winner.

The situation currently includes a fresh legal turn. JPMorgan Chase is reported to be close to joining other banks in paying over US$400 million to settle claims of price fixing in the market for certain local government bonds, which would close a long legal fight without a jury verdict. For investors who want the banking giant as part of a wider basket, XLF, MGV and VFH are three ETF tickers that include the stock among broader holdings.

Prefer to pick the companies yourself? Start with 37 high quality undervalued stocks.

State Street Financial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLF)

XLF leans heavily toward large US financial companies. Diversified banks, including JPMorgan Chase, are the single biggest slice at 23.9% of the fund, and JPMorgan Chase alone accounts for 11.12% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 you put in holds roughly US$111 in the bank. Berkshire Hathaway is a larger holding at 13.4%, while Visa at 8.74% pulls some of your money toward payment processing and fee based activity rather than deposits and lending.

A risk for JPMorgan Chase is that spending on marketing, technology and AI could climb faster than revenue and weigh on margins. XLF holds other financial industries such as insurance, asset management and exchanges, which do not rely on the same expense decisions at the bank, so that pressure is partly isolated to JPMorgan Chase. You still depend heavily on conditions for big US finance groups rather than a mix that stretches into sectors such as healthcare or consumer staples.

Vanguard Morningstar Mega Cap Value ETF (MGV)

Pharmaceutical and semiconductor holdings give MGV a very different mix around JPMorgan Chase. Micron Technology and companies in pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and consumer staples retail sit alongside integrated oil and gas and aerospace and defense groups. JPMorgan Chase is the second largest position at 4.18% of the fund, so each US$1,000 in MGV holds about US$42 in the bank and the rest in other large US value stocks. No single holding dominates the portfolio, which keeps the fund’s result driven by several industries rather than one company.

Management at JPMorgan Chase has described current trading conditions as close to as strong as they get, with solid activity and high volumes. If that tone cools across financials, banks inside MGV could all feel it, while semiconductor, healthcare and energy holdings depend more on chip demand, drug markets and global energy conditions instead. Investors using MGV get JPMorgan Chase plus sizeable exposure to sectors that face different business cycles and policy trends than large US banks.

Vanguard Financials ETF (VFH)

VFH gives JPMorgan Chase a real share of your money at 10.09% of the portfolio. Each US$1,000 you invest puts about US$101 into the bank, which keeps its specific moves important to your outcome. The rest goes into a wide spread of financial industries, with exposure to diversified banks, payment processors, brokers, multi sector holdings and insurers. About 86% of VFH overlaps with XLF, so it looks similar, although Berkshire Hathaway and Visa still pull a meaningful slice of your money toward different parts of global finance.

A long period of heavier marketing, technology and AI spending at JPMorgan Chase could outpace revenue growth and narrow profit margins. VFH cannot fully blunt that company specific pressure, because JPMorgan Chase is still the largest position. However, the other 90% of assets tied to different financial businesses gives you additional levers for how your overall financial sector bet plays out.

Your JPMorgan Chase mix comes first

Your real choice is how tightly you want JPMorgan Chase tied to your other holdings. XLF and VFH both put roughly US$100 of every US$1,000 into the bank, and both are built mainly from financial industries, so they sit closer to a sector style bet. XLF is more top heavy with 80 holdings. VFH spreads you across 431 positions, which softens the impact of any single bank compared with XLF.

MGV is different. Only about US$42 of each US$1,000 goes into JPMorgan Chase and the rest leans toward semiconductors, healthcare and energy. All three funds charge low fees. Your first question is whether you want most of your money with financial companies that can face legal issues like the recent bond case, or a mix where banks are just one piece.
